title: Largest 1-Bordered Square
statement: `grid` is a rectangular matrix whose cells are each `0` or `1`. Among all square blocks of contiguous cells inside `grid` (any side length from 1 up), consider those whose outermost ring of cells (top row, bottom row, left column and right column of the block) consists only of `1`s; the cells strictly inside that ring may hold anything. Return how many cells the biggest such block covers (its side length squared), or `0` when no block qualifies, which happens only if `grid` has no `1` at all.
constraints: Every row of grid has the same length
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every square and walking its four edges costs O(m·n·k²) for side bounds k. The edges are just runs of `1`s, so if every cell already knows how long the run of `1`s ending at it is (going left and going up), one square's border can be checked in O(1).

A square is fixed by its bottom-right corner and its side `side`. Its bottom edge and right edge end at that corner, its top edge ends at the top-right corner, and its left edge ends at the bottom-left corner.

## Approach

1. Build `left` and `up` with one padding row and column of zeros, so `left[i][j]` / `up[i][j]` describe `grid[i - 1][j - 1]`.
2. Scan cells row by row. A `0` keeps both counts at zero.
3. For a `1`, extend the run from the neighbour: `left[i][j] = left[i][j - 1] + 1`, `up[i][j] = up[i - 1][j] + 1`.
4. The bottom and right edges allow at most `side = min(left, up)`. Try sides from there down to `best + 1`: the square fits when the top row run `left[i - side + 1][j]` and the left column run `up[i][j - side + 1]` both reach `side`.
5. Return `best * best`.

## Example 1, step by step

Every border cell gives `side = 1`, which sets `best = 1` at the first cell. The centre is `0`, so neighbours of it get short runs. At the bottom-right cell `left = 3` and `up = 3`, so `side = 3`; the top row run `left[1][3] = 3` and the left column run `up[3][1] = 3` both reach 3, so `best = 3` and the answer is `9`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m·n·min(m, n)): each cell tries at most min(m, n) sides, each in O(1).
- Space: O(m·n) for the two run tables.

## Pitfalls

- Only the border must be `1`; the interior may contain `0`s.
- Return the area (`best * best`), not the side length.
- The answer is `0` only when the grid has no `1`; a single `1` already counts.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left[i][j]` | consecutive `1`s ending at the cell, going left |
| `up[i][j]` | consecutive `1`s ending at the cell, going up |
| `best` | largest valid side found so far |
| `side` | side length being tried for the current bottom-right corner |
| `topRow`, `leftColumn` | run lengths along the square's top edge and left edge |
